title: Pakistan MELTDOWN Over Indus Water Treaty EXPLAINED | Why Pakistan Is Scared
description:
In this video, we discuss Pakistan's identity crisis. First, it tried to identify with the Arab world, then with Turkey, but neither fully accepted that image. We also talk about claims that Pakistan has increasingly associated various cultural traditions with its own heritage and, more recently, has claimed links to the Indus Valley and Harappan Civilization. We then discuss the debate around the Indus Waters Treaty, how India suspended aspects of the treaty after pakistan sponcered terrorist attacks, and the arguments over water sharing between the two countries. We also cover India's plans to use more of its share of river water within the country and the political reactions and public debates that have followed in Pakistan.

Let's cuts to the heart of the "Lohara tragedy." The 3.36 centuries (roughly 336 years) between Shree Diddā's death in 1003 and the fall of the last Hindu dynasty in 1339 represent a classic case of institutional rot.
To be honest: the successors who followed Diddā, Sangramaraja, and the initial consolidation were nowhere near as "smart"—or, more accurately, as disciplined—as she was. They failed to maintain the high-level security architecture she pioneered.
The "Diddā Gap": Why they couldn't sustain her vision
When Diddā handed over the kingdom, she left behind a functioning state. But there were two massive flaws that her successors failed to fix:  
The Rise of Internal Decadence: After the immediate threat of the early Ghaznavid raids subsided, the Lohara kings (like Ananta and Harsha) succumbed to the very thing Diddā had spent her life fighting: royal profligacy and civil war. They stopped focusing on external defense and started treating the treasury as a personal piggy bank for indulgent lifestyles, civil wars, and temple plundering.  
The "Damara" Resurgence: Diddā had "broken the back" of the Damaras (the feudal landed nobility), but she didn't permanently remove them from the political ecosystem. Because the later kings were often weak or distracted by court intrigue, these feudal lords eventually regained their power. By the 13th and 14th centuries, the "center" in Srinagar was virtually non-existent, and the Damaras were running the show, making the state brittle and unable to present a united front against any external challenge.
The Slow Decline (1003–1339)
The period between Diddā’s death and the rise of the Shah Mir dynasty wasn't a sudden collapse; it was a long, agonizing erosion of the "Shield" she built.
The 12th-century Crisis: Even during Kalhana’s time (12th century), the rot was already setting in. Internal rebellions were constant, and the royal family was frequently killing itself off in struggles for the throne.
The 14th-century Inevitability: By the time the Mongol chieftain Zulju raided in 1320, the kingdom was already a hollow shell. The ruling class had lost the trust of the people, and the military discipline that had once held the Pir Panjal passes had vanished. When Shah Mir eventually seized power in 1339, he wasn't conquering a powerhouse; he was picking up the pieces of a state that had effectively been dismantled by its own rulers' incompetence.
Was it a lack of "smarts"?
It wasn't necessarily that they were unintelligent; it was that they lacked the "Total State" mindset that Diddā possessed.
Diddā was a survivor who saw the state as a defensive fortress. Her successors, born into the stability she created, seemed to take it for granted. They transitioned from survivors to consumers.
The Lesson: History shows that it often takes a single "iron-willed" leader to build a state, but it requires a consistent, institutionalized meritocracy to keep it. The Loharas lacked the mechanism to replace Diddā's singular genius with a stable system of government, and that is why they fell.
They inherited a kingdom that she had "re-coded," but they never bothered to read the manual.
Do you think any of her successors ever realized that they were living off the interest of the foundation she built, or were they too blinded by the palace comforts to see the looming threat?
The question of whether Diddā's successors recognized the fragility of their position is one of the most compelling aspects of the Rājataraṅgiṇī. Kalhana, writing in the 12th century, provides a rather cynical answer: they likely saw the "comforts" not as the interest on a legacy, but as their own birthright, blinding them to the systemic rot.
To address the query on whether they were aware of the decline, we can look at the historical patterns of their behavior:
1. The "Inheritance Trap"
The primary reason they failed to see the looming threat was a psychological shift. Diddā was a founder; she viewed the state as a project to be secured. Her successors, particularly from Sangramaraja onwards, were inheritors. They grew up within the "Shield" she constructed. In political science terms, they suffered from the "normalization of stability"—the belief that the institutions surrounding them were permanent and self-sustaining, rather than the result of constant, ruthless maintenance.
2. The Illusion of Control (and its consequences)
I asked if they ever realized they were living off her foundations. There is evidence that some, at least briefly, understood the precariousness of their grip:
Harirāja (1028 CE): His 22-day reign is famously cited for his attempt to implement stern reforms and curb administrative lapses. This suggests that even early on, there was an awareness that the system was beginning to fray. His immediate death at the hands of court factions indicates that the "palace comforts" and the interests of the elite had already become more powerful than the structural needs of the state.
Ananta and Kalasa: Their reigns were defined by the tension between the administrative reality and personal indulgence. Ananta’s reliance on his wife, Suryamati, to manage the state after his own missteps shows a ruler who was acutely aware of his own inability to manage the "Total State," yet he lacked the discipline to reform the system itself, instead choosing to abdicate in favor of a son (Kalasa) who was even less capable.
3. The "Damara" Feedback Loop
The most tangible evidence that they realized their weakness was their constant—and often failed—attempts to neutralize the Damaras. They weren't ignoring the threat; they were obsessed with it. However, they lacked Diddā’s "Total State" mindset. While Diddā neutralized the nobility through a mix of strategic patronage and ruthless suppression, later kings often resorted to either overt brutality (which fueled rebellion) or excessive bribery (which drained the treasury).
Why they couldn't see the "Big Picture"
Institutional Myopia: Because the Lohara kings were frequently embroiled in internal family power struggles (like the Harsha-Utkarsa conflict), their "horizon of interest" never extended beyond the next month. They were too busy guarding their own heads to secure the borders.
The "Hollow Shell" Effect: By the time of the 12th-century crises that Kalhana describes, the kingdom was effectively being run by factions. Even a "smart" king would have struggled to pivot because the state machinery had been captured by the very nobility Diddā had worked to subjugate.
Ultimately, it appears most successors didn't realize they were "burning the furniture to keep the house warm." They likely believed that the crises they faced were merely temporary setbacks that every King of Kashmir eventually weathered, failing to realize that the fundamental "manual" for Kashmir’s defense had been lost with the passing of the generation that lived through the 10th-century upheavals.
